title: How to find the centre of your fabric
subtitle: Locating the starting point so a design lands centred in the hoop
excerpt: Finding the centre of the fabric before stitching ensures the design lands in the middle of the piece and not crowded against one edge. There are two methods: fold-and-crease for small pieces and thread-basting for large or linen pieces where creasing would distort the weave.
sourceNotes: Standard cross-stitch setup convention documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework (1880s), Internet Archive, and confirmed in modern cross-stitch manuals. The fold-and-baste method is universal.

glossaryTerms.definition: A temporary running stitch used to mark a centre line or grid on cross-stitch fabric. Worked in a contrasting thread and removed after the stitching is complete.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

content.text: Finding the centre of the fabric before stitching is the one step that prevents a finished piece sitting off-centre in its hoop or frame. The chart marks the centre with arrows pointing at a grid intersection, and the fabric's centre is the point where those chart arrows correspond. Everything else is counted out from there.
There are two reliable methods. The fold-and-crease method is quick and works well on
Aida
. The basting-thread method takes a few minutes longer and is better for linen or large pieces where a fold crease would interfere with the weave or distort an area you will stitch over.
Method 1: fold and crease
Fold the fabric in half vertically, lining up the side edges. Run your fingernail lightly along the fold to leave a faint crease. Do not iron the crease into linen; a light fingernail mark is enough.
Unfold and fold in half again in the other direction (horizontally). Crease again.
Unfold completely. Where the two crease lines cross is the centre of the fabric. Mark this point with a small stitch in a contrasting thread, or simply begin your first stitch here.
Method 2: basting thread
Thread a needle with a contrasting single strand of
floss
(do not knot the end).
Stitch a loose
basting
running stitch along the fold line from top to bottom of the fabric, going over and under alternate holes. This marks the vertical centre line.
Repeat in the other direction (left to right) to mark the horizontal centre line.
Where the two basting lines cross is the centre of the fabric. Begin the first stitch of the design at the chart centre, counting from this point.
Remove the basting threads when the design is finished by pulling them from the stitched edge. They should slide out without disturbing the cross-stitches.

items.symptom: The design is noticeably off-centre after a few rows
items.cause: The fabric was not folded evenly, or the crease was used to count from rather than the exact crossing point.
items.fix: Measure the distance from the edge of the fabric to the crease on both sides. If they differ, find the true midpoint by measuring and use that point instead of the crease.

items.symptom: The basting thread is difficult to remove after stitching
items.cause: The basting thread was knotted, or it passed under and over too many stitches.
items.fix: Always work basting without a knot. Pull gently with one hand while using the other to keep the finished stitches flat.

content.text: What to try next
Once the centre is established, the next step is
reading the chart
to know how many squares to count outward before beginning the first stitch. The chart arrows point at the chart centre; match those to the fabric centre and start from there.
